title: The Iliad, Homer
subtitle: 8th century BC
subject: litterature
description: Not the whole Trojan War: 51 days of wrath. Achilles withdraws, Patroclus dies, Hector falls. Homer shows how glory can turn brutal, then human again.

hero.hook: One word opens the poem: wrath. And the whole war tips over.

blocks.text: People often assume the **Iliad** tells the whole **Trojan War**. In fact, the poem attributed to **Homer** covers only **51 days**, deep inside the tenth year of the siege. The war set a Greek coalition against the city of Troy, and it began with the abduction of Helen. But the first subject of the poem is not Troy: it is the **wrath** of **Achilles**, the best of the Greek warriors.

The title comes from **Ilion**, the other name for Troy, a city on the coast of what is now Turkey. Beneath the gods, the duels and the violence, Homer asks a simple question: what is glory worth when everyone dies? The poem does not celebrate war without reservation. It shows the human cost.

sections.title: Why Achilles walks away from the fight

blocks.text: The mythical pretext is well known: **Paris**, a Trojan prince, carried off **Helen**, queen of Sparta. **Agamemnon**, king of Mycenae and leader of the Greeks, commands the coalition. But the poem opens on a crisis inside the Greek camp. Agamemnon humiliates Achilles by taking **Briseis**, his captive. For Achilles, that is an attack on his [[timè]], the public honor owed to a warrior's worth. Without timè, the hero has no reason left to fight.

blocks.caption: The quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon, the starting point of the whole Iliad

blocks.text: Achilles withdraws to his tent. Worse: he asks his mother **Thetis**, a sea goddess, to obtain a Greek defeat from **Zeus**, king of the gods. He wants to prove that the army cannot do without him. His resentment matters more to him than the survival of his comrades. The war becomes a question of ego first, not only of conquest. Homer shows that the anger of one man can tip the fate of a whole army.

sections.title: Patroclus dies, and the anger changes

blocks.text: Without their champion, the Greeks give way. The Trojans, led by prince **Hector**, son of King Priam and the great defender of Troy, even threaten the Greek ships. **Patroclus**, the closest companion of Achilles, borrows his armor to frighten the enemy. Achilles agrees, but forbids him to push too far and chase the Trojans back to the walls of Troy.

In the Iliad, the gods get hurt too. The warrior **Diomedes** wounds **Aphrodite**, goddess of love, in the hand. **Ares**, the god of war, has to flee the field screaming. Even Olympus feels the violence of the battlefield.

Patroclus disobeys. Hector kills him, helped by **Apollo**, the archer god. The anger of Achilles began as a social wound. Now it becomes something else. Timè no longer drives him: grief arms the hero. Homer shows how one emotion can turn destructive.

sections.title: Achilles against Hector: glory turns brutal

blocks.text: Achilles comes back. Armed by **Hephaestus**, the smith god, he enters his [[Homeric aristeia]], a long sequence in which a hero performs superhuman feats. He kills Hector in front of the walls of Troy. Then he ties the body to his chariot and drags it through the dust, in full view of the prince's family. The humiliation is extreme.

blocks.caption: The Trojan War on a Greek vase: glory, violence and fate all mixed together

blocks.text: For the Greeks, denying **funeral rites** means stepping outside humanity. Honoring the dead with a burial is a sacred duty. Achilles, the absolute hero, becomes almost an animal. Homer shows the price of [[Mênis (wrath) in Greek culture]]. The first word of the poem, *Mênis*, announces an almost cosmic theme. The wrath of Achilles unsettles the order of the world as much as the war itself does.

sections.title: Priam before Achilles: humanity comes back

blocks.text: Old King **Priam**, the father of Hector, crosses the enemy lines alone to kiss the hands that killed his son. Facing that broken father, Achilles thinks of his own father, **Peleus**, whom he will never see again. He gives the body back and grants a truce for the funeral. The poem closes on the burial of Hector. The [[Trojan Horse]], the trick Odysseus used to get inside the city, does not appear in it at all.

events.title: Achilles and Agamemnon quarrel
events.detail: Achilles leaves the fight for lack of timè.

events.title: Death of Hector
events.detail: Achilles wins, then defiles the body.

events.title: Priam and Achilles
events.detail: Shared grief brings back a little humanity.

blocks.text: The **Iliad** is not a handbook of glory. In **51 days**, Homer shows how anger destroys, then how two enemies recognize each other in the same pain. The poem ends on the peace of the dead, not on victory.
